1.pericope_label: Paul an apostle, not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father

schools.summary: Explain the letter’s vehemence by the gravity of the offence, and identify the teachers as Jewish believers who invoked the practice of Peter, James and John — a practice explained as condescension to Jewish weakness rather than doctrine; and gather the scriptural testimonies to the raising and the session at the right hand.

Set the epistle against the false teachers who came in after Paul left, reconstructing their case against him — that he was converted last, never saw Christ, and had persecuted the Church, while they had been conversant with the apostles.

Ground the apostolic title in the calling of God rather than the judgment of men, note that the opponents conceded him the ministry and denied him only the apostolate, and distinguish the two senses of the word so that Paul stands equal to Peter and the Twelve; and add that he neither took the honour to himself nor ran before he was sent.
Insist that this was no common call of an ordinary minister but an extraordinary call from heaven, with neither the qualification nor the designation coming through any human mediation.

Preface the letter with the history of the province and set out the chapter as a single argument for an apostleship independent of men; distinguish the two prepositions as source and channel and answer the objections from Ananias and from the commissioning at Antioch; and derive the bluntness from the Judaizing charge that Paul was no apostle because not one of the Twelve, the resurrection clause supplying his qualification.

Observe that Paul is elsewhere sparing with the title and name the places where he omits it, and take the closing clause as marking what an apostle exists to do, which is to bear witness to the resurrection.
Use the verse against Marcion by demanding the credentials of an apostle absent from the Gospel’s list, and press that a choice made after the ascension would impute improvidence to Christ.

debates: What the two prepositions distinguish, and whether the distinction survives the cases of Ananias and of the commissioning at Antioch (Ellicott).
In which sense “apostle” is claimed — the wider use that covers Barnabas and James, or the strict one that puts Paul level with the Twelve (Calvin, Ellicott).
Whether the appeal of the false teachers to Peter, James and John was fair, Chrysostom conceding the fact and denying that their forbearance was doctrine.
Whether an apostleship conferred after the ascension can stand at all, which Tertullian raises as an objection in Marcion’s mouth in order to answer it.
outliers: Tertullian alone treats the verse as a problem about Paul’s credentials rather than a proof of them.
Chrysostom alone reconstructs the opponents’ appeal to the practice of the Jerusalem apostles and explains it away as condescension.
Luther alone puts a speech in the false teachers’ mouths and answers it as they framed it.
Wesley alone counts the letters in which Paul withholds the title, and gives a reason for each.

2.pericope_label: The brethren, the churches of Galatia, and the salutation: who gave himself for our sins

schools.summary: Explain the joint authorship by the weight of numbers, contrary to Paul’s usual practice; defend the title “church” for a body that has largely revolted, on the ground of the external marks it retains; heap up what Christ did not give in order to show what he did; and make remembrance of our relation to Christ the cure for error.

Deny that Paul needed the brethren’s authority and take their inclusion as a sign of sympathy only; note the deliberate bareness of a salutation that elsewhere begins with praise, and that this letter is circular; distinguish the three prepositions rendered “for” so that the death is a sacrifice with respect to sins, on behalf of sinners and in their stead; and question whether the doxology states a fact rather than offers a wish.

Extend the first verse’s distinction into three degrees of sending — of men, of God without man, of God through a man — so that the brethren sign as fellow-soldiers rather than apostles; and press the “gave himself” on both sides, against what Christ did not receive and what he was not given for, calling the words thunderclaps against every kind of righteousness.

Restrict “this present evil world” to the Jewish economy of carnal ordinances, with a lexical argument for rendering the adjective “oppressive”; and observe that Paul withholds from these readers the titles saints, elect and churches of God.

debates: Why Paul associates all his companions in the address — for the weight their concurrence would carry (Calvin) or merely to show he had their sympathy, since he needed no help in his own defence (Ellicott).
Whether a body that has largely abandoned the gospel can still be called a church, which Calvin raises and answers from the external marks, while Wesley notes the titles Paul does withhold from them.
What “this present evil world” denotes: the Jewish ritual economy specifically (Clarke), or the present age in general (Wesley, Robertson).
Whether the doxology ascribes a glory already possessed or asks for one — Ellicott would supply “is” rather than “be”.
outliers: Ellicott alone contradicts the received explanation of the joint address, and alone argues that the doxology is a statement rather than a wish.
Calvin alone asks whether the Galatian congregations deserve the name of churches, and alone gives a rule for when the name may be withheld.
Clarke alone confines the evil world to the Mosaic economy, and alone cites a lexical case for rendering the adjective as “oppressive”.
Luther alone builds a threefold scheme of sending out of the first verse’s two prepositions.

6.pericope_label: I marvel that ye are so soon removed unto another gospel, which is not another

schools.summary: Note the deliberate mildness of the opening word and date the letter from “so soon”; attribute the calling to God the Father, Christ’s part being mediate agency; press the present tense and the desertion metaphor; survey the renderings of the following clause and settle for the sense that this was no gospel at all, the conjunction meaning “except that” and the verb meaning to reverse a thing into its opposite.

Explain the gentleness as deliberate strategy — a fatherly and even excusing manner towards the fallen, with the thunder reserved for the seducers, because the purpose is to raise up rather than to crush.

Take the rebuke as milder than deserved; build an exhortation on the present tense, that they are only in the act of falling and must retreat at once rather than advance a step; hold that what they are leaving is Christ himself, the corrupted doctrine leaving only an imaginary Christ; and rank subversion as a worse crime than corruption. Add that there is but one gospel and that this trumpet gives no uncertain sound.
Aggravate the defection by observing that they turned not merely from the apostle who was the instrument of their calling but from God who directed it.

Refer “him that called you” to the apostle himself; identify “another gospel” with one of the spurious written gospels then in circulation, several of which urged circumcision and the Mosaic law; and describe the rival message as heavy tidings that set acceptance with God on impossible terms.

Concede the abolition of the ancient law but derive it from the Creator’s own dispensation, foretold by the prophets and dated by Christ at John the Baptist; and turn the Galatians’ own confusion into proof that Paul had preached no second god.

debates: From whom the Galatians had been removed — the apostle who called them (Clarke), God who directed the preaching (Henry), or God the Father specifically, with Christ as mediate agency (Ellicott).
What “another gospel” denotes: one of the apocryphal written gospels then circulating (Clarke, alone), or the Judaizing message (all the others).

How to construe “which is not another” — as a correction guarding against there being two gospels, or as contempt for a doctrine that is no gospel at all, with Barnes reviewing the older renderings and Ellicott making the conjunction mean “except that”.
What the present tense concedes, and whether it makes the letter an intervention before the fall is complete (Calvin, Ellicott, Robertson).
outliers: Clarke alone identifies the rival gospel with a written apocryphon and cites a catalogue of more than seventy.
Tertullian alone uses the Galatian error as evidence about the identity of the God who gave the law.
Calvin alone turns the tense into a direct exhortation to stop where they stand.
Barnes alone dates the epistle from the word “soon”, and alone names the source of his remark about Paul’s mildness.

8.pericope_label: Though we or an angel preach another gospel, let him be accursed; do I now persuade men?

schools.summary: Treat the supposition as impossible and the curse as real, no name or office screening the offender; regard as devils those who bring another gospel; read the condemned teaching as the true gospel corrupted by human additions rather than flatly contradicted; and find in the last verse two proofs, that Paul did not accommodate himself to men and, more strongly, that he was not the gospel’s author but its steward.

Mark the supposition as extreme and improbable; weigh the disputed preposition and settle for “contrary to” against the sense Protestant commentators have preferred, since the issue was an opposition of principles; explain the repetition by the shift from what was preached to what was received; and read the last verse as a denial of conciliating men, with “yet” meaning still, at this late stage of a career already set against the age.

Soften the anathema into a direction that such a teacher be denied countenance and separated from the Church’s communion, with judgment following impenitence; render “persuade” as courting favour; and press on the reader the impossibility of pleasing God and the world together.

Take the curse at full force as an excommunication of every teacher without exception, and note that the second curse is deliberately reworded from what was preached to what was received, to forestall the plea of misunderstanding; and supply the tone of a man whose preaching had already earned him his nation’s hatred.
Allow two senses for the disputed verse — that Paul acted in obedience to God and not men, or that he aimed to bring others into obedience to God and not men.
Apply the anathema to the transmitted creed, so that what is delivered by the Church is to be held against any later teaching, even from the teachers themselves or from an angel of light.

debates: Whether the anathema is an imprecation or a direction for discipline — Clarke takes it as the latter, citing a Greek father, where Luther and Calvin take it at full force.

What the preposition in “other than that which we preached” means: “besides”, which would condemn additions, or “contrary to”, which would condemn only opposition — a choice Ellicott identifies as confessionally loaded, deciding for “contrary” where Calvin decides for additions.
To what “as we said before” refers — an earlier visit (Ellicott) or the immediately preceding verse (Barnes), who argues Paul could not have anticipated the perversion while among them.
What “persuade” means when its object is God: teaching (Gill), courting favour (Clarke, Ellicott), or an attempt at persuasion the tense marks as unsuccessful (Robertson).
outliers: Cyril alone uses the verse as a rule for transmitting a creed rather than as a weapon in the Galatian dispute.
Clarke alone tries to reduce the anathema to a disciplinary measure.
Ellicott alone states the confessional interest attaching to the preposition before deciding against the side he belongs to.
Luther alone reconstructs the excuse the wording of the second curse is designed to block.

11.pericope_label: The gospel I preached is not after man: I received it by the revelation of Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Note that Paul still calls them brethren and uses the word to win a hearing; call the claim of direct revelation the hinge of the whole question, proved from a narrative rather than asserted; concede that a man may have taught him without prejudice to the revelation, since a human teacher only gives weight to a public ministry; and rule out Gamaliel, the apostles and Ananias in turn.

Observe that this is the first time he calls them brethren at all; deny any spark of human invention in the gospel; distinguish the two verbs by tempo, receiving at once against being taught slowly; and fill in from the narrative what the first revelation contained, with the promise of more to come.

Weigh the solemnity of the verb “certify” and render “after man” as an adjective, the gospel being not human in nature or origin; answer the objection from Ananias by denying that he taught Paul anything doctrinal; and dispute whether one revelation is meant, one side placing it at the conversion and defending its sufficiency, the other denying that a single unveiling is required at all.

Deny that “not after man” means only “not earthly”, since the opponents claimed a heavenly doctrine too, and make it mean that Paul learned it by no earthly means whatever — not by hearing, reading or writing, as everyone else does; and note that the denial is confirmed by an oath.

debates: What the objection from Ananias proves — Barnes denies he taught Paul anything of the doctrine, while Calvin allows that a man may have taught him and denies that this touches the revelation.
Whether “the revelation of Jesus Christ” means a single unveiling at the conversion, whose sufficiency Ellicott defends, or whether the grammar leaves the number open (Robertson).
How “received” differs from “was taught” — as gift against process (Ellicott) or as suddenness against gradualness (Wesley).
What “not after man” excludes: human invention, a human standard of judgment, or every earthly means of learning whatsoever (Luther, who rejects the weaker senses).
outliers: Wesley alone remarks that Paul has withheld the name “brethren” until this point.
Calvin alone answers the Ananias objection by concession rather than denial.
Luther alone points out that the opponents also claimed a heavenly doctrine, so that the phrase must mean more than it seems.
Robertson alone refuses to fix the revelation to a single occasion, citing Paul’s use of the same verb for what he received about the Lord’s Supper.

13.pericope_label: My former life in Judaism: how I persecuted the church of God and profited above my equals

schools.summary: Trace the vocabulary — “Judaism” as a Maccabean term for the religion set against Hellenism, the verb for wasting as the word Christians themselves used of Saul, “equals” as contemporaries at the rabbinic school — and take the traditions of the fathers for the oral law that grew up beside the Pentateuch, the progress covering zeal and observance as well as knowledge.

Make the narrative part of the argument, a man so attached to his fathers’ customs being untearable from them except by a miracle, and read “the traditions of my fathers” not as the corrupting additions but as the law of God itself received through parents and ancestors; and note that deeper proficiency in Judaism made him the more violent a persecutor.

Agree that the traditions meant are Moses’ own law received as an inheritance, not pharisaical inventions; and turn the biography into an argument against the Judaizers — a man who had every reason to glory in legal righteousness abandoned it.

Take the traditions as the unwritten additions over and above the written law; restrict the boast to superior skill in those traditions rather than superior obedience to the pure law of God; and explain that the readers knew the story because they knew what had happened in Judea.

Read the persecution as providence — the Spirit gave the former enemy more epistles than the rest so that the doctrine might be beyond question — and answer the amazement of those who remembered him by pleading ignorance, since he had thought the preaching of Christ destroyed the Law.

debates: What “the traditions of my fathers” denotes: the oral law of the elders (Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley, Barnes) or the law of God itself as handed down (Calvin and Luther, against the rest).
What Paul claims to have surpassed his contemporaries in — skill in the traditions only (Clarke) or zeal and ritual strictness as well as knowledge (Ellicott).
How the Galatians knew this history: from Paul’s own preaching, from its general notoriety, from Jews of the dispersion, or because they were themselves Jews acquainted with Judean affairs.

Why the biography is introduced at all — as proof that the conversion was divine (Calvin), as proof that the gospel was not learned from men (Barnes), or as an argument against the value of legal righteousness (Luther).
outliers: Cyril alone treats the persecutor’s past as the reason for the size of his correspondence, and alone puts the plea of ignorance into Paul’s mouth as a reply to the amazed.
Calvin and Luther alone deny that the disputed traditions are the pharisaic oral law.
Robertson alone observes that the word for wasting the church is the one the Damascus Christians used of Saul himself.
Ellicott alone offers a modern parallel for the backward look at one’s contemporaries.

15.pericope_label: God separated me from my womb and revealed his Son in me; I conferred not with flesh and blood

schools.summary: Fix “from my mother’s womb” at birth rather than before it; hear the irony in a verb that makes Paul a Pharisee separated now for the gospel; divide over whether the Son was revealed within him or in his case, one side building a sequence of flash, retirement and preaching, the other following Lightfoot for the objective sense; and leave the site of the Arabian retreat undetermined while placing it between the two Damascus visits.

Refer the whole to sovereign good pleasure; read the disputed construction as a Hebrew idiom meaning simply “to me”, so that the revelation was given in order to be preached; take “flesh and blood” for human counsel of every kind; and answer the silence of Acts about the three years by saying the historian omits them, as he omits much else.

Grant that this is an unconditional predestination consistent with God’s justice and mercy; and divide over “flesh and blood”, one voice rejecting the reading that makes it the promptings of Paul’s own heart and the other adopting exactly that reading.
Turn the revelation into a test for the reader: it will little avail us to have Christ revealed to us if he is not also revealed in us.
Take the retirement into Arabia as the refutation of the charge that Paul was a mere pupil of the apostles who had lived under the law, since he began preaching at once on a heavenly calling alone.

debates: Whether “separated me from my mother’s womb” means before birth or from birth, which Ellicott decides from parallel usage.
Whether the Son was revealed “in” Paul inwardly (Gill, Ellicott, and Henry’s application) or “to” him objectively (Calvin, Robertson, with Barnes keeping to the event and Wesley taking both).

What “conferred not with flesh and blood” excludes — human advisers only, which Clarke insists on and Calvin assumes, or a man’s own reason and inclinations as well, which Wesley adds and Clarke expressly denies.

Where in Arabia Paul went, and how the three years are to be reconciled with Acts: by allowing that the historian omits them (Calvin) or by fitting an early and fruitless visit to Jerusalem into them (Gill).
outliers: Wesley alone concedes an unconditional predestination in this case, and alone takes both senses of the disputed phrase.
Robertson alone hears the Pharisaic sense of “separated” behind Paul’s use of it.
Ellicott alone builds a three-stage psychology of the conversion out of the sequence of clauses.
Barnes alone lists later converts whose early lives were as unpromising as Paul’s.

18.pericope_label: After three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter; I saw no other apostle save James

schools.summary: Weigh the reckoning of the three years and warn that the phrase will not bear a precise chronology; press the unusual verb for the visit, which means to learn by personal inquiry and gives us the word history, and take the purpose as acquaintance rather than instruction; prefer the reading Cephas and concede that the passage does suggest Peter’s leadership; and let the apostleship of James follow from his identity rather than settle it, rejecting the theory that the Lord’s brethren were his cousins.

Derive “history” from the same verb and complain how far modern histories have fallen from it; deny that the visit was for religious knowledge, since Paul already knew as much and had preached three years; treat “brother” as kinsman on the authority of earlier writers; and confine the oath to the fact that he had seen only two of the apostles.

Count the three years from the beginning of the apostolic office and make the shortness of the stay the argument; report the ancient traditions about James and reject the cousin theory precisely because he is here numbered among the apostles; and take the oath as an occasion to state when swearing is lawful.
Ask why an oath was needed and answer from the contempt in which Paul was held by his own converts, drawing the consolation that lesser men need not wonder at being disbelieved.

debates: From what point the three years are counted — the departure for Damascus, the return from Arabia, the conversion, or the beginning of the apostolic office — and whether the phrase can bear any precise reckoning at all (Ellicott doubts it).

Whether James the Lord’s brother was an apostle, and whether that settles his identity: Calvin argues from the apostleship against the cousin theory, Ellicott argues from the identity to the sense of the title, and Robertson allows the wider use.
What “brother” means — kinsman or cousin (Barnes, Clarke, Wesley, and the view Calvin reports as more probable) against Ellicott’s firm conviction that this is untenable.
How far the oath reaches: over the whole narrative of the chapter (Barnes, Calvin) or only over the extent of Paul’s contact with the apostles (Clarke, Ellicott).
outliers: Clarke alone turns the etymology of “history” into a complaint about historians.
Ellicott alone concedes that the passage supports the Roman argument for Peter’s primacy, and alone uses the three days in the grave to loosen the sense of “three years”.
Calvin alone lets the word “apostle” overrule what he otherwise thinks the likelier account of James.
Luther alone reads the oath as evidence of how little the Galatians thought of Paul, and applies it to preachers in his own day.

21.pericope_label: Into Syria and Cilicia, unknown by face to the churches of Judaea, who glorified God in me

schools.summary: Trace the route from Damascus to Tarsus and pronounce the narrative in agreement with the history; insist that Paul was converted elsewhere and had preached in no congregation of that country; and conclude that he owed everything to God and nothing to men, having entered the ministry by no rite the Church has ever used — against those since who prefer to display human credentials.

Explain the order of the two provinces as unchronological and dismiss both the invented extra journey and the alleged contradiction; distinguish Judaea from Jerusalem and take the plural of churches as evidence of how early the Church was organised; read “in Christ” as a real and personal relation rather than a label; make the tense of the hearing continuous; and treat the closing praise as the right form of admiration for an eminent Christian, which passes through him to God.

Show what the ignorance of the Judean churches forestalls, that Paul might have learned the gospel from them; qualify the language of destroying the faith, which cannot be destroyed but only weakened in the minds of the weak, the will rather than the deed being expressed; and turn the churches’ praise into a caution against worshipping the men whom God has adorned with gifts.
Call the whole church of Judaea as witness that Paul preached the very faith he had persecuted, and that what they glorified God for was the preaching of faith and not any teaching of circumcision.

debates: Whether the sequence “Syria and Cilicia” conflicts with the order of travel in Acts — Clarke and Robertson find simple agreement, Barnes explains the omitted episode as immaterial, and Ellicott denies that the order is chronological at all.
What “the faith” means at this date: the gospel (Robertson) or the single doctrine of faith in Christ, the body of doctrine being still unformed (Ellicott).
Whether faith can be destroyed, which Calvin denies while allowing that its influence on weak minds can be lessened.

What the praise of the Judean churches is doing in the argument — proving his approval by the mother churches (Calvin, Barnes), reproaching the Galatians by contrast (Gill), or supplying a body of witnesses (Luther).
outliers: Clarke alone uses the passage against ministers who value human credentials, noting that no bishop or presbyter ever laid hands on Paul.
Ellicott alone takes the plural “churches of Judaea” as dated evidence for how quickly the Church organised itself.
Calvin alone qualifies the verb “destroyed” so that faith itself is not made destructible.
Calvin and Ellicott alone read the closing verse as a rule for how eminent Christians should be admired.
